title: His mother stood (John 19:25–27)
hook: Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple as his mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, remember me: a dying thief asked for one thing and was promised a garden. Your line was this day in paradise. Who did you remember out loud? Day sixty-five.

Think about the worst hospital waiting room you've ever sat in. Nothing to do. Nothing to fix. You stay because leaving is unthinkable. Now go back to the hill. Most of the men who followed Jesus have scattered. But John's Gospel slows down and names who is still there, standing by the cross: his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. And one disciple, the one the Gospel only ever calls the disciple whom Jesus loved. They can't stop it. They can't even get close enough to wipe his face. They stand. Today's word is three words from that verse.
screen: `NOTHING TO FIX. YOU STAY.` → `FOUR WOMEN AND ONE DISCIPLE.` → `THEY STAND.`

segments.voice: Then Jesus, who can barely breathe, spends some of his last words on this. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, behold thy son." And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." And John adds: "And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Woman sounds cold to us. It isn't. It's the same word he used for her at the wedding at Cana, a word of respect, and some readers hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis. There are two ways to hear this moment, and Catholics hold both. The first is simple and human. A dying son makes sure his widowed mother will have a home. That alone is worth sitting with. The second is bigger. The Gospel never names the beloved disciple. Tradition says it was John, but leaving him unnamed lets every disciple stand in his place. So Catholics read it as Jesus giving his mother to all of us, and they call Mary the Mother of the Church. Pope Paul VI gave her that title during the Second Vatican Council. Then there's the word stood. In the Latin Bible it's stabat, and a medieval hymn opens with it: Stabat Mater, the mother stood. It's sung on Good Friday and during the Stations of the Cross. She didn't faint. She didn't leave. She stood.
screen: `WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON.` · `A SON MAKES SURE HIS MOTHER HAS A HOME.` · `THE UNNAMED DISCIPLE IS EVERY DISCIPLE.` · `STABAT MATER: THE MOTHER STOOD.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand beside someone who is suffering. Settle and breathe. Bring one person to mind who is going through something you can't fix. Picture yourself not fixing it. Just standing near them, the way Mary stood. Notice how hard it is to do nothing but stay. Then think of one small way to be there this week: a visit, a call, sitting with them in silence. If you pray, you can ask Mary to stand with them too. The bell holds the time.
His mother stood. Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple, and, Catholics say, to all of us. Today's word.
Your line: behold thy mother. Today, look after someone else's mother, or someone who mothered you, in one small, practical way. Day sixty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics sing or pray the Stabat Mater during the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, and honor Mary as Mother of the Church on the Monday after Pentecost.

fork.setup: you're dying, and your mother is standing below you. you have only a few words left. what do you do with them?
options: give her to your friend, and your friend to her.
fork.reveal: "woman, behold thy son... behold thy mother." he spends his breath making sure she has a home, and Catholics hear him giving her to everyone.

original.note: Latin: the mother stood. the opening of a medieval hymn sung on Good Friday.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary was sad at the crucifixion.
what it means: she stood, when most had fled, and her son gave her to his friend as his mother and his friend to her as her son.
what a scholar hears: the beloved disciple is never named, so every disciple can stand in his place. that is why Catholics call Mary Mother of the Church.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 19:26–27 given from memory; confirm.
John 19:25: whether 'his mother's sister' and 'Mary of Cleophas' are one or two women is debated; the script lists them as the Douay-Rheims order reads, allowing either.
'Woman' as a term of respect and the Cana echo (John 2:4); the Genesis echo is a patristic and modern reading. Confirm.
Paul VI proclaimed Mary Mother of the Church on 21 November 1964, at the close of the third session of Vatican II; memorial on the Monday after Pentecost since 2018. Confirm.

Stabat Mater: 13th-century, often attributed to Jacopone da Todi; used as the sequence for Our Lady of Sorrows and commonly sung at the Stations. 'Sung on Good Friday' is customary rather than prescribed; confirm.
